verses.text: In the beginning, God  created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness.
God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.
God said, “Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.”
God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse; and it was so.
God called the expanse “sky”. There was evening and there was morning, a second day.
God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear”; and it was so.
God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”. God saw that it was good.
God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so.
The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a third day.
God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;
and let them be for lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth”; and it was so.
God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.
God set them in the expanse of the sky to give light to the earth,
and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day.
God said, “Let the waters abound with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.”
God created the large sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
There was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.
God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind”; and it was so.
God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good.

God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
God said, “Behold,  I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.

footnotes.content: Before there was a single thing to count or name, God was already there. The Hebrew word behind "created" is bara, a making the Scriptures reserve for God alone — not reshaping what was already lying around, but calling into being what had never been. I have found this a steady place to stand when life feels formless: the beginning belongs to Someone, not to chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darkness, deep water, and emptiness — and right there in the middle of it, God's Spirit hovering. The old Hebrew word for hovering is the same one Moses used of an eagle stirring over its nest in Deuteronomy 32:11. Nothing is so unfinished that the Lord will not brood over it with the tenderness of a parent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God does not wrestle the darkness into light; He simply says the word, and light is. I have noticed that the Lord still works this way with us — He speaks, and something in a shadowed heart begins to see. Creation is, in a sense, God's first sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God looked at the light and called it good before He separated it from the dark. He is not in a hurry past His own work; He pauses to enjoy it. There is a quiet lesson here for anyone who only ever inspects what they have made for flaws.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives the light and the dark their names — day, night — as a father might name children in his house. Then comes the first evening and morning, the rhythm that would carry every human life after it. Even the dark gets a name and a place in His ordering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God speaks an expanse into the middle of the waters, a wide room between the deep above and the deep below. It is the sort of careful separating a woodworker does, making space where there was only flood. Order begins as a gift of room to breathe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The waters are divided, and the text adds simply, "and it was so." No struggle, no committee, no negotiation — the word of God and the obedience of what He made. I find that phrase restful; the world is not held together by my effort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The expanse is named "sky," and a second day closes. Notice that God names what He makes before He fills it — sky first, then birds; sea first, then fish. He prepares a home before He brings anyone into it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The waters under the sky are told to gather in one place so that dry land can appear. What was once all ocean becomes a shore, a place to stand. I think of how often the Lord clears a small patch of solid ground for someone who thought they were drowning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Earth and seas are given their names, and again God sees that it is good. The land is not merely leftover space after the water was moved; it is named, and naming in this book means belonging. He is not an absent landlord of the ground beneath our feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grass, herbs, and fruit trees — each with its own seed inside it. God builds the future into the thing He makes, so that life would not need a fresh miracle every spring. There is generosity in a design that keeps giving after the first gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earth does exactly what it was told: grass, seed, fruit, each after its kind. The repeating phrase "after their kind" is not a cage but a family resemblance, an orchard that stays an orchard. God's world is orderly enough to be trusted and varied enough to be enjoyed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A third evening, a third morning. The refrain is almost plain enough to skip, and yet it is the sound of a world being built steadily rather than all at once. The Lord is patient with His own work, and He is patient with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lights are given a task beyond shining: to mark seasons, days, and years. Time itself is a gift hung in the sky, so that human life would have festivals to keep and planting to plan. Later Israel would set her whole calendar by these same lights.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their purpose is stated simply — to give light on the earth. Not to be worshipped, not to be decoded for fortunes, just to shine for the sake of those below. I like that the sky's great lamps are, in the end, servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two great lights are made — the greater to rule the day, the lesser to rule the night — and the stars are added almost in passing. Moses never even uses the Hebrew names for sun and moon here, only "greater" and "lesser," so that no one would mistake them for gods. The heavens are a household with lamps, not a pantheon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sets the lights in the expanse Himself, placing them like a lamp on a stand. They did not drift into position; they were put there, on purpose, with the earth in view. Even the far-off stars are arranged with someone's window in mind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To rule the day and the night, to divide light from darkness — and God sees that it is good. Ruling here is not domination but keeping order, the way a night watchman keeps a street safe. The dark is not left lawless; it too has a keeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fourth day closes over a sky now furnished with lights. Heaven and earth have been made, then shaped, then filled — and still no one is there to see it but God. He works faithfully even when there is no audience, which is a fair definition of character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The waters are told to abound with living creatures, and the sky to be crossed by birds. It is the first sound of creaturely busyness in the story — swarming, fluttering, moving. God seems to delight in abundance rather than bare sufficiency.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The great sea creatures are named first, the ones an ancient sailor would have feared most, and God makes them too — then every small swimming thing and every winged bird. Nothing wild falls outside His making or His care. Even what frightens us has a Maker who called it good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before God gives a single command to a human being, He blesses fish and birds with the words "be fruitful, and multiply." Life is meant to spill over its banks. Readers today hear an echo of that first blessing in every crowded tide pool and every spring nest — abundance is not an accident here, it is a benediction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fifth day ends, and the sea and air are already full. The story keeps that quiet evening-and-morning beat, as if God is going home satisfied each night. There is a restfulness in a Creator who is never behind schedule.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the earth itself is told to produce living creatures — livestock, creeping things, wild animals. The ground that grew grass now grows something that breathes. God works through what He has already made, layering gift upon gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Animals of the field, livestock, and everything that creeps — each after its kind, and all of it good. The small unglamorous creatures are listed alongside the impressive ones. I take comfort that the Lord's eye for goodness is not limited to the magnificent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every other creature came at a command; this one comes after a pause — "Let us make man in our image." The plural has kept readers listening for centuries, some hearing a heavenly council, others the Trinity. What is plain is the deliberation: God stops and considers before He makes us, and then gives us a share in caring for the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times in one verse the word image lands, like a hammer driving a nail: in His own image, in God's image, male and female. This is the ground of every human dignity — not strength or usefulness, but a family likeness. The person beside you, however overlooked, carries that mark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God blesses the man and woman and gives them work: be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it, have dominion. Dominion here is the caretaking of a gardener, not the greed of a conqueror — they rule on behalf of the One who owns it all. It is a calling, and a heavy one, given to those just made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first provision is food: every seed-bearing herb and every fruit tree, given freely before anyone has asked. Notice that God does not merely permit eating; He says, "Behold, I have given you." The table is set before the need is spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The animals and birds and creeping things are given green herbs too, so that no living thing is left out of the provision. The same hand that made the lion feeds it. I have learned to read this as a quiet statement about the breadth of God's care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six times God called His work good; here, with humanity in the garden, He looks at everything and calls it very good — tov me'od, a phrase that carries the sense of delight. This is not merely adequate craftsmanship but a Father pleased with what He has made. Whatever else you believe about yourself today, the Maker's verdict over His work was joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
